newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Continental in exclusive 20-year pact with Boeing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Continental in exclusive 20-year pact with Boeing.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc. said Tuesday it has agreed to buy 35 wide-body jets from Boeing Co., becoming the third major U.S. carrier to sign an exclusive supplier agreement with the airplane maker.

Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune said the airline will pay a "deep discount" from list prices estimated at about $3 billion in a 20-year pact as it joins Delta Air Lines Inc. and American Airlines in inking long-term pacts with Boeing.

"My successors are guaranteed they won't be paying more for airplanes than the competitors," said Bethune, adding that Boeing guaranteed the Houston-based carrier will not pay more than its rivals for the new airplanes.
Under the deal, Continental will buy five Boeing 777-200 aircraft and 30 767-400ER aircraft through the year 2004, with options for additional 777 and 767 purchases to be negotiated in the future.

The carrier also pushed up delivery of five 777 aircraft already on order, with the 10 777 aircraft to be delivered from September 1998 through May 1999. The 30 767 aircraft will be delivered in mid-2000 through the end of 2004.
The new wide-body aircraft will replace Continental's fleet of six DC10-10 and 31 DC10-30 aircraft, which will be retired as the new Boeing aircraft are delivered.
Last year, AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, the nation's second-biggest carrier, pledged to buy up to 630 jets from Boeing over the next 20 years in a deal that could be worth more than $35 billion.
In March, Delta, the third-biggest domestic carrier, signed a similar contract to make Boeing its exclusive supplier for 25 years in a deal valued at more than $15 billion.

The deals, which shut out Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium, angered European officials considering whether to approve Boeing's planned $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. Last month, the European Commission issued a formal statement of objection to the merger, listing the exclusive supplier deals as among its prime concerns.
The latest pact also drew fire from Airbus Industrie, which in recent weeks was shut out of talks with Continental as Boeing nailed down the deal, an Airbus spokesman said.

"We had talked with them, but in the end it came down to just a conversation between Boeing and Continental without Airbus," said David Venz, a spokesman with Airbus Industrie North America. "Clearly, this has the appearance of Boeing making a grab at locking up the American market."

Continental, the nation's fifth-largest carrier, is in the middle of heated contract talks with its pilots union, but Bethune said there were no contingencies in its deal with Boeing to delay deliveries if the talks break down.
"We didn't use this as a lever" to put pressure on the pilots, Bethune said, adding that he still hoped to wrap up the union talks by July 1, when the contract with 4,000 Continental pilots expires.
Continental, which operates hubs in Newark, N.J.; Houston; Guam and Cleveland, plans to deploy the new wide-body airplanes on its expanding international routes and transcontinental flights.

Continental's "A" shares were down $2.375 at $34 a share and its "B" shares were off $2 at $33.50 a share, while Boeing shares were up $1.50 at $57.50 a share in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
